column13: Yet nonetheless the wording of the holy Zohar remains difficult: 'let the body delight itself as is fitting for it, let it eat meat, etc.,' for why eat meat to provoke the accusation of the evil inclination that could lead to spiritual breakdown? column15: And concerning this it is said (Psalms 104:15): “And wine gladdens the heart of man,” for from this stems that giddy joy, because it conceals and confounds the mind until he fails to perceive an Overseer in the world. Opposite this it is stated here: “Rooms shall you make in the ark” — meaning that he must conduct every matter with sober composure, like one who builds a house and sets within it defined boundaries and distinct chambers for each specific use.

column11: Chullin 132b: ‘Rav Ḥisda says: Gifts of the priesthood may be consumed only when they are roasted, and they may be consumed only with mustard seasoning. What is the reason for this halakha? column15: So surrounding lights shield man from evil, enduring eternally. column11: Avodah Zarah 3a: ‘Immediately, each and every gentile will take materials and go and construct a sukka on top of his roof. column11: Kiddushin 40a: ‘But the Holy One, Blessed be He, does not link an evil thought to an action, as it is stated: “If I had regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not hear” (Psalms 66:18). But how do I realize the meaning of the verse: “Behold I will bring upon these people evil, even the fruit of their thoughts” (Jeremiah 6:19)? In the case of an evil thought that produces fruit, i.e., that leads to an action, the Holy One, Blessed be He, links it to the action and one is punished for the thought as well. If it is a thought that does not produce fruit, the Holy One, Blessed be He, does not link it to the action.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 9, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Kiddushin 40a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and "a good thought the Holy One combines with deed" (Kiddushin 40a); for we yearn to perform the mitzvah, our abstention being due solely to circumstance beyond our control, Scripture accounting...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column13: This aligns with what is taught in the first chapter of Kiddushin (40a): that a good thought is joined by the Holy One to action, so that even if one intended to perform a mitzvah but was prevented by circumstances beyond his control, Scripture reckons it as if he performed it; but an evil thought is not joined to action, because sin operates strictly through physical action, which is finite and bounded like this physical world of action (Olam Ha'Asiyah); whereas thought possesses no physical boundary or perimeter at all.
column15: Meaning, each person holds an ordered book engraved in his heart from the providential circumstances Hashem leads him through, seeing He is the Cause of all causes; yet striving in concrete action cannot be taken gratis, but only through full payment; for active mitzvot embody deep Torah wisdom beyond human intellect, which Hashem enclothed within physical actions.

column11: Shabbat 63a: ‘The Gemara asks: What is the meaning of the phrase in that verse: “And that think upon His name”? Rabbi Ami said: Even if one merely planned to perform a mitzva, and ultimately due to circumstances beyond his control did not perform that mitzva, the verse ascribes him credit as if he performed it. The Gemara continues in praise of those who perform mitzvot: Rav Ḥinnana bar Idi said: Anyone who performs a mitzva as it was commanded, others do not apprise him of bad tidings, as it is stated: “He who keeps the commandment shall know no evil thing” (Ecclesiastes 8:5).’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 9, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 63a) to illuminate his exposition here (“for we yearn to perform the mitzvah, our abstention being due solely to circumstance beyond our control, Scripture accounting it as if we performed it (Shabbat 63a); wherefore through the Hallel...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 71:10: ‘"Zilpa the maidservant of Leah gave birth to a second son to Jacob" (30:12). “Leah said: In my happiness, as women will be happy for me; she called his name Asher” (Genesis 30:13). “Leah said: In my happiness [beoshri], as women will be happy for me” – saying: ‘Happy is the one who merited this.’ Rabbi Levi said: Asher never stayed the night in an inn. column13: Concerning which the Sages already declared (Bereishit Rabbah 10:7, Vayikra Rabbah 22:1, and Kohelet Rabbah on "Moreover the profit of the earth is in all things") that all were created for the world's necessity, and likewise in Shabbat (77b) and Berakhot (31b). column11: Taanit 8b: ‘§ The Gemara relates: In the days of Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani there was a famine and a plague. The Sages said: What should we do? Rather, let us pray for mercy for the plague, and as for the famine, we must bear it. column11: Sotah 5a: ‘Rabbi Yoḥanan said: The Hebrew word for person, adam, written: Alef, dalet, mem, is an acronym for efer, dust; dam, blood; and mara, bile, alluding to man’s insignificance. Similarly, the Hebrew word for flesh, basar, written: Beit, sin, reish, is an acronym for busha, shame; seruḥa, putrid; and rimma, worm, also alluding to his insignificance. There are those who say that the letter sin of the word basar actually is referring to a different word, sheol, the netherworld, as it is written with the Hebrew letter shin. The letter sin is phonetically similar to the letter samekh, the first letter of the word seruḥa, but is orthographically similar to the letter shin, the first letter of the word sheol. The dispute is whether the acronym should be based upon the pronunciation or upon the way it is written.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 9, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sotah 5a) to illuminate his exposition here (“alluding to the name Basar (flesh) as written in Sotah (5a): acronym of Bushah (shame), Seruchah (foulness), Rimah (worms); and through sinning and feeling contrite shame, meriting shame through...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column11: Gittin 43a: ‘Rabba bar Rav Huna went back and placed an interpreter before him so that he could tell the public that he had been wrong, and he interpreted a verse homiletically. Therefore, I retract my previous statement and say that although the Sages said that in the case of one who betroths half a woman, she is not betrothed, however, if there was a half-maidservant half-free woman who was betrothed, then her betrothal is a valid betrothal. What is the reason for the distinction? column11: Kiddushin 38a: ‘This is as it is written: “And the children of Israel ate the manna forty years until they came to a settled land; they ate the manna until they came to the borders of the land of Canaan” (Exodus 16:35). column11: Ketubot 67a: ‘GEMARA: Abaye said: The fifty dinars mentioned in the mishna is referring to fifty provincial dinars, each of which is worth one-eighth the amount of a standard dinar. From where do I know that this is so? From the fact that the latter clause teaches: If there are sufficient resources in the charity fund, the charities provide more for her, furnishing a dowry and her other needs according to her dignity. And we say: What is this fund? Raḥava said: The charity fund. And if it enters our minds to say that the mishna is referring to fifty actual, i.e., standard, dinars, if there are sufficient resources in the fund, how many standard dinars do we give him? Fifty standard dinars is already a sizable sum to distribute as charity. Rather, conclude from this comment that the mishna is referring to fifty provincial dinars.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 9, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Ketubot 67a) to illuminate his exposition here (“specifically emphasizing "my portion" (chuki), each individual according to his legitimate standard, like that impoverished aristocrat accustomed to fattened chicken and aged wine (Kesubos 67a);...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column11: Sukkah 29a: ‘The Sages taught in another baraita: When the sun is eclipsed, it is a bad omen for the other nations. column11: Sefer Yetzirah 1:1: ‘YAH, ADONAI of Hosts, God of Israel, Living God and King of the World, EL SHADDAI, Merciful and Gracious, High and Exalted, Dwelling Ever Above, Holy Is His Name—He carved 'Work of Creation' is not the abstract verb bara 'to create' used in [Genesis 1:1]. Instead, the SY prefers verbs relating to the processes of craftsman and artisans, in particular stonemasons: chaqaq 'to carve, chisel', chatzav 'to hew', shaqal 'to weigh', yasad 'to found', yatzar 'to form, shape, fashion'—the latter providing the name of the book, Sefer Yetzirah, literally the 'Book of Forming' but conventionally rendered the 'Book of Creation'. and created His World 'and created His World' in this verse. In these versions, God simply chaqaq 'carved', with no object expressed overtly. See also SY 5:4, where God simply yasad 'founded', with no overt object.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Sefer Yetzirah 1:1) to illuminate his exposition here (“And this is the esoteric mystery of the three dimensions: text (Sefer), author (Sofer), and reading/recitation (Sippur, Sefer Yetzirah 1:1); for there are three aspects within every Hebrew letter:...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column11: Bamidbar Rabbah 20:24: ‘“Behold, a man from the children of Israel came and brought near to his brethren the Midyanite woman, before the eyes of Moses, and before the eyes of the entire congregation of the children of Israel. And they were weeping at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting” (Numbers 25:6). “Behold, a man from the children of Israel came and brought near to his brethren” – what did he see that led him to do so? It is to teach you that he neither accorded deference to Heaven nor to people. In his regard it is stated: “A spiteful and arrogant man, scoffer is his name; he acts with spiteful ire” (Proverbs 21:24). She said to him: 'I will submit only to Moses your teacher, as my father is a king.' He said to her: 'I am as great as he is. I will bring you before their eyes.' He seized her by her forelock and brought her to Moses.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bamidbar Rabbah 20:24) to illuminate his exposition here (“and therefore the Sages expounded (Bamidbar Rabbah 20:24) on the verse "Now shall it be said of Jacob and of Israel: What has God wrought!" (Bamidbar 23:23); that Israel's inner partition is...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And the preparation for the cure began through a banquet, and the completion of deliverance arrived through Esther's banquet, inviting the King and Haman, "the King" being the King of the Universe, uniting the Holy One and His Shechinah, from which emerged the sacred Purim feast; and because a holy feast had not yet been codified, prosecution attached to every banquet, which is why Haman—the supreme accuser—was invited; he imagining it was for his honor, whereas it was orchestrated to destroy him.
column15: And the Generation of the Flood, expanding into worldly pleasures to the utmost limit without introducing eyes of discernment into Malchut, brought about the total collapse of the entire natural order; for the Blessed Name overturned the celestial alignment and natural laws completely, as stated in Midrash Rabbah (34:11) that the constellations ceased their orbits throughout the twelve months of the Flood.

column11: Numbers 23:23: ‘Lo, there is no augury in Jacob,No divining in Israel: Jacob is told at once,Yea Israel, what God has planned.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Numbers 23:23) to illuminate his exposition here (“and therefore the Sages expounded (Bamidbar Rabbah 20:24) on the verse "Now shall it be said of Jacob and of Israel: What has God wrought!" column13: “Hashem his God is with him” ibid.—this pertains specifically to Torah scholars. Divination kesem, Numbers 23:23—is based on celestial orbits and astrology, requiring analytical intellect, hence: “neither is there any divination against Israel”—the scholars; and enchantment nachash, ibid.—superstitious omens like bread falling from one’s mouth Sanhedrin 65b, lacking intellect—does not exist “in Jacob,” the common folk.
column15: For surely “God is not a man that He should lie, neither the son of man that He should repent,” but it was providential design to build a world worthy of: “This one pleases Me.” And even after declaring “This one pleases Me,” creation had to traverse further rebukes akin to shattered worlds—the Dispersion and Sodom (see section 1).

column11: Bamidbar Rabbah 20: ‘“He said to Balak: Stand here with your burnt offering, and I will be happened upon there” (Numbers 23:15). “The Lord happened upon Bilam, and placed speech in his mouth, and said: Return to Balak, and so shall you speak” (Numbers 23:16). “He built seven altars…stand here with your burnt offering…. The Lord happened upon Bilam, and placed speech in his mouth” – like a person who places an iron bit in an animal’s mouth and restrains it, and leads it to wherever he wishes. So, the Holy One blessed be He restrained his mouth. When he said to him: "Return to Balak" and bless them, he said: ‘What, am I going there to disappoint him [Balak]?’ He sought to go off on his own. The Holy One Blessed be He placed an iron bit for him. “Return to Balak, and so you shall speak.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bamidbar Rabbah 20) to illuminate his exposition here (“and therefore the Sages expounded (Bamidbar Rabbah 20:24) on the verse "Now shall it be said of Jacob and of Israel: What has God wrought!" (Bamidbar 23:23); that Israel's inner partition is...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column12: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 3:14 (§2)
column13: For as is known from Bereishit Rabbah (parashah 14), there are five levels to the soul: Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah, Chayah, and Yechidah. Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah correspond to thought, speech, and action, as I have written at length elsewhere: action is centered in the liver, which is full of blood, and "the blood is the Nefesh"; speech resides in the heart, as written: "and speaks truth in his heart," where the spirit of life (Ruach) dwells, as is known.
column15: And this is what is written: “And for man there was not found a helper opposite him”; for when inanimate, vegetable, and animal entities enter man and he elevates them, subsumed into his being, and he strides with that vitality to serve Hashem and proclaim the Shema, an entire burnt-offering is truly forged from all those forces.

column11: Sefer Yetzirah 1:5: ‘Ten SEFIROT BELIMAH—Their measure is ten; they have no edge. Depth ‘depth’ here is based on the metaphor of ʽamuqqah ‘deepness’ as a symbol of divine mystery, as found in Biblical poetry, ex. [Job 11:8], [Psalms 64:7], [Ecclesiastes 7:24]. It could perhaps be understood in the SY as meaning 'dimension', 'mystery', or 'mystical dimension'. of Beginning, Depth of End; Depth of Good, Depth of Evil; Depth of Above, Depth of Below; Depth of East, Depth of West; Depth of North, Depth of South. The Unique Lord EL, the faithful king, governs them all from His Holy Abode, forever and ever and ever.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Sefer Yetzirah 1:5) to illuminate his exposition here (“And this is the "depth of good" (omik tov) among the ten depths enumerated in Sefer Yetzirah (1:5); which I heard explained: "depth of good" and "depth of evil" signify that which in its inward...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And this is man's first superiority: in that he possesses potential deficiency—the inclination toward evil—yet is safeguarded from it; whereas the second superiority is by virtue of his higher intrinsic stature and closer proximity to Hashem. And as we noted, whoever carries vulnerability to deficit exhibits proof of higher spiritual stature; meaning that the essential soul of Israel surpasses the angels, deriving from an exalted source within the Father's essence—as the Zohar states: one who exhales, exhales from his innermost depths—wherefore they merited to be called "children," as explained above.
column15: Therefore, even though human labor is minute at the ultimate root—for in the absolute depths free will has no autonomous reality save within the perimeter of mortal grasp, and what is it worth? — nevertheless the Blessed Name deprives no creature of its reward, and no good intention of man is ever lost before the Holy King (Zohar Terumah 156b).

column11: Pesachim 2a: ‘The Gemara raises an objection: “And God called the or Day, and the darkness He called Night” (Genesis 1:5). Apparently, or is day. The Gemara rejects this proof as well. This is what the verse is saying: God called the advancing light Day. As stated previously, the word or can also be a verb; in this context, God called the beginning of that which eventually brightens, Day. The Gemara challenges this explanation: However, if that is so, the continuation of the verse, “and the darkness He called Night,” should be understood to mean: He called the advancing darkness Night, even before it is actually dark. However, this cannot be the correct interpretation of the verse, as we maintain it is day until the emergence of the stars.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Pesachim 2a) to illuminate his exposition here (“And in this world which resembles the night (Pesachim 2a), which is darkness and the deeds of the wicked; precisely out of this darkness will they merit the radiant light of the World to Come...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: For it is known that every reality is structured across Space, Time, and Soul (Olam, Shanah, Nefesh), as written in Sefer Yetzirah: in the dimension of Space (Olam), the qualities of day and night are manifest as the light of the sun and the light of the moon [and the stars, which are also categorized as light as stated in Pesachim (2a), serve the function of "depart from evil," as written in Berakhot (43b) that the light of the moon provides the visibility of three companions so that one is not seen by harm and does not suffer injury, avoiding the pitch darkness that resembles the deeds of the wicked].
column15: The explanation of this is: How could it ever enter one’s mind that the Blessed Name might delight in the deeds of the wicked? Rather, at the inception of creation darkness preceded light; yet how can darkness apply to the Blessed Name?

column11: Deuteronomy 32:12: ‘The ETERNAL alone did guide them,No alien deity alongside.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Deuteronomy 32:12) to illuminate his exposition here (“the good having been severed from the evil, where "Hashem alone did lead him, and there was no strange god with him" (Devarim 32:12), without any mixture of evil; meriting the light of Atzilus,...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And this is the indestructible stature of Israel which can never be severed: that they are "the portion of Hashem" (Devarim 32:9), their root deriving from Atzilus, where there is no existence of evil or free choice whatsoever; and while for every Jew there exists this concealed root, King Shlomo was entirely cleaved there; and therefore the Bat Kol said "for you must choose, etc.," for in that supernal realm your human choice has no bearing at all.
column15: And this is what is written (Deuteronomy 32:10): “He found him in a desert land... He encompassed him, He instructed him, He guarded him as the apple of His eye.” Therefore, since creation came into being solely through the longing of Israel who desired Heavenly honor, the nations can never claim “You are plunderers”; for Israel is the essential core of creation.

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 3:6: ‘“God called the light, Day” – are “light” and “day” not the same thing? This is bewildering. It is taught: The light that was created during the six days of Creation cannot illuminate by day, because it would make the orb of the sun seem dim [by comparison], nor can it [illuminate] at night, as it was created to illuminate only during the day. Where is it, then? It was stored away, and is designated for the righteous for the future, as it is stated: “The light of the moon will be like the light of the sun and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, like the light of the seven days” (Isaiah 30:26). This is bewildering: “Seven [days]”? Are they not three? Is it not so, that the lights were created only on the fourth day? It is, rather, like a person who says: This and that I am preparing for the seven days of the wedding feast.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 3:6) to illuminate his exposition here (“meriting the light of Atzilus, which is the primordial light of the seven days of Creation hidden away for the righteous in the Future (Bereishis Rabbah 3:6; Chagigah 12a); when they will sit with...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And the Foreknowledge of Rosh Hashanah is prior to spiritual exertion, concerning that which is destined to be good and righteous from its root. While Yom Kippur is after spiritual exertion, and even after man sins, nonetheless "they shall be as white as snow" (Isaiah 1:18), because they are like these years pre-ordered from the six days of Creation (Shabbat 89b); meaning fixed and enduring from eternity through the truth of Hashem's will, and it emerges that they never sinned nor turned aside at all from the truth of His will.
column15: For all redemptions in this world flow solely from the subterranean reservoir bubbling forth from that which is prepared for the ultimate future, as the Targum translates “A Song of Ascents”: “to raise up the deep,” for the “deep” signifies the hidden treasury where all future goodness and transcendent light are stored.

column11: Chagigah 12a: ‘And for whom did He conceal it? For the righteous people in the future, as it is stated: “And God saw the light, that it was good” (Genesis 1:4), and “good” is referring to none other than the righteous, as it is stated: “Say of the righteous that it shall be good for them, for they shall eat the fruit of their actions” (Isaiah 3:10). When the light saw that it had been concealed for the righteous, it rejoiced, as it is stated: “The light for the righteous shall rejoice” (Proverbs 13:9).’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Chagigah 12a) to illuminate his exposition here (“meriting the light of Atzilus, which is the primordial light of the seven days of Creation hidden away for the righteous in the Future (Bereishis Rabbah 3:6; Chagigah 12a); when they will sit with...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And the Midrash notes that "the Almighty spread His cloud..."; the Name Shaddai is elucidated elsewhere in our writings as denoting the contraction (tzimtzum) of the manifest Shechinah to mortal capacity, as in Chagigah (12a): "for I said to the world: Enough (dai)"; meaning that divine revelation should not expand boundlessly, which would blind and overwhelm finite recipients; this Name hinting at the limiting boundary Hashem set so His light is measured to human capacity, which is the purpose of creation.
column15: As written: “See now that I, even I, am He, and there is no god with Me” — meaning the concealing Name Elohim will dissolve, leaving the Name Havayah alone, such that every instance of Elohim becomes absorbed in Havayah, unveiling the primordial light hidden throughout the six days of creation.

column11: Berakhot 17a: ‘Rav was wont to say: The World-to-Come is not like this world. In the World-to-Come there is no eating, no drinking, no procreation, no business negotiations, no jealousy, no hatred, and no competition. Rather, the righteous sit with their crowns upon their heads, enjoying the splendor of the Divine Presence, as it is stated: “And they beheld God, and they ate and drank” (Exodus 24:11), meaning that beholding God’s countenance is tantamount to eating and drinking.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 17a) to illuminate his exposition here (“when they will sit with "their crowns—namely their cleaving at their root unto Him—upon their heads, and enjoy the splendor of the Shechinah" (Berachos 17a), which is the Supernal Shechinah...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: As written in Berakhot (17a): in the World to Come the righteous sit with crowns on their heads and derive pleasure from the radiance of the Shechinah. So too, the Sabbath embodies lucid, permanent awareness of the Name of Heaven [which is fixed and established, as stated in Pesachim 117b; and this is not the place to elaborate], as written in the holy Zohar (II, 88b): "What is Shabbat? It is the very Name of the Holy One, Blessed be He."
column15: And as my revered father explained regarding the dictum (Pesachim 8a): Why are the righteous before the Shechinah compared to a candle before a torch, and not to a candle before the sun — because “of what use is a lamp in broad daylight?” where its light is nullified and swallowed entirely within the solar brilliance; whereas a candle before a torch, being an integral part thereof—since from the joining of many candles a great torch is formed—does not lose its identity completely.

column11: Sanhedrin 90a: ‘MISHNA: All of the Jewish people, even sinners and those who are liable to be executed with a court-imposed death penalty, have a share in the World-to-Come, as it is stated: “And your people also shall be all righteous, they shall inherit the land forever; the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, for My name to be glorified” (Isaiah 60:21). And these are the exceptions, the people who have no share in the World-to-Come, even when they fulfilled many mitzvot: One who says: There is no resurrection of the dead derived from the Torah, and one who says: The Torah did not originate from Heaven, and an epikoros, who treats Torah scholars and the Torah that they teach with contempt.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 90a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and "all Israel have a portion in the World to Come" (Sanhedrin 90a), meaning even the sinners of Israel, for all are tzaddikim; as they stated in Nedarim (31b): one who vows regarding the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: But in truth they cleave to the living God, and all their deeds are for the sake of Heaven; and even though the revealed [surface] of the deed is not so, the discerning one understands that the depths of their hearts truly cleave to Him. And this is the exposition of the “expounders of reshumos” [in Perek Chelek, Sanhedrin 105a]: that “all of them [Israel] have a share in the World to Come,” all those of the seed of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov — except for Bilaam, the “expounders of impressions” (dorshei reshumos) taught that all of the seed of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov have a share in the World to Come — Bilaam alone excepted (cf.
column15: And this Israel alone can achieve, as stated in the Gemara (Sanhedrin 58b): “A non-Jew who observes the Sabbath is liable to death, as it is written (Genesis 8:22): ‘Day and night they shall not cease’”; for the Sabbath is an exclusive covenant between Him and the Children of Israel.

column11: Nedarim 31b: ‘Conversely, if he said: Benefiting from those who are circumcised is konam for me, he is prohibited from deriving benefit even from uncircumcised Jews and he is permitted to derive benefit from the circumcised of the nations of the world, as the term uncircumcised is used only to name the nations of the world, as it is stated: “For all the nations are uncircumcised, but all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart” (Jeremiah 9:25), and it says: “And this uncircumcised Philistine shall be” (I Samuel 17:36), and it says: “Lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised triumph” (II Samuel 1:20). These verses indicate that ordinary gentiles are referred to as uncircumcised, regardless of whether they are actually circumcised.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Nedarim 31b) to illuminate his exposition here (“as they stated in Nedarim (31b): one who vows regarding the uncircumcised is forbidden unto uncircumcised Israelites, for all are termed circumcised even if uncircumcised in physical fact. And so...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: For a nail, although external and capable of being trimmed, is nonetheless an organic part of the body itself. But the children of Israel, who even when uncircumcised are categorized as circumcised (Nedarim 31b), possess no dross organically attached to their essential bodies at all; their dross resembling merely a full stomach emitting foul odor: once evacuated and the foul waste expelled from within the body, the blemish is gone; and there is no inherent dross or foulness in the essence of an Israelite, there being merely an internal foreign waste, while their interior possesses the expulsive force to reject and cast it out, banishing the foulness.
column15: The nations, however, assert that the world was generated something from something (yesh mi-yesh), like ordinary physical sowing and breeding. And even though the creation of Adam HaRishon was ex nihilo (yesh me-ayin), regarding this the nations claim that the Blessed Name was compelled to create existence, reasoning that when the Holy One desired to be designated as “King,” He was, as it were, forced to create a universe possessing moral free will.

column11: Berakhot 17a: ‘After his prayer, Rabbi Alexandri said the following: May it be Your will, Lord our God, that You station us in a lighted corner and not in a darkened corner, and do not let our hearts become faint nor our eyes dim. Some say that this was the prayer that Rav Hamnuna would recite, and that after Rabbi Alexandri prayed, he would say the following: Master of the Universe, it is revealed and known before You that our will is to perform Your will, and what prevents us? On the one hand, the yeast in the dough, the evil inclination that is within every person; and the subjugation to the kingdoms on the other. May it be Your will that You will deliver us from their hands, of both the evil inclination and the foreign kingdoms, so that we may return to perform the edicts of Your will with a perfect heart.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 17a) to illuminate his exposition here (“as written in Berachos (17a): "It is revealed and known before You that our will is to perform Your will, and who prevents us? The yeast in the dough!"; and as is known the teaching of the Rambam...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column12: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:39
column13: There (Berakhot 4b): "He who juxtaposes redemption to prayer" etc.: Redemption (Ge'ulah) is the rescue of man from his soul's oppressors—namely, bodily lust and the "yeast in the dough" (the evil inclination), which is compared in Berakhot (17a) to the subjugation of foreign empires; and only in the wake of that deliverance can authentic prayer take place.
column15: Only from the union of both aspects—the mystery of the son and the mystery of the servant—does prayer become operative, mediated through Malchut. The elucidation of this is: at the essential root Israel are designated children of the Omnipresent, blessed be He; yet the Blessed Name erected a concealing garment through which it appears to man that he holds active agency and labor to fulfill Heavenly honor and reveal light out of darkness.

column11: Mishneh Torah, Divorce 2:20: ‘When a man whom the law requires to be compelled to divorce his wife 14:8), a man who was married to a woman for ten years without her bearing a child (Hilchot Ishut 15:7), a man who becomes afflicted by [constant] bad breath or an odor from his nose, one who becomes a collector of dog feces, a miner of copper or a tanner or one who becomes a leper (Hilchot Ishut 25:11-12) or a priest who marries a divorcee (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 17:7). does not desire to divorce her, the court should have him beaten until he consents, at which time they should have a get written. The get is acceptable. This applies at all times and in all places. or to the era when the Sanhedrin (the High Court of Law) was in power.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this commentary and philosophical-halakhic exposition (Mishneh Torah, Divorce 2:20) to illuminate his exposition here (“and as is known the teaching of the Rambam (Hilchos Geirushin 2:20) on why "the court coerces him until he says: 'I desire it'"; and although he sins in deed whereby he is labeled wicked,...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column12: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Large Beth; Small Beth 16 (§4)
column13: As Maimonides wrote (Hilchot Geirushin 2:20) on coercing a man until he says "I am willing," for the essential soul never desires sin; see there. Sin being merely accidental, repentance is effective, an accidental circumstance being capable of eradication. Evil being only an accidental mate to sinners, wherefore a divine decree for evil can be rescinded, while a decree for good is never rescinded (Berakhot 7a).
column15: And this is: “And the man said: This time it is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman” — meaning: although for all other creatures I would not lower myself to raise them, for this one who is bone of my bones I am compelled to humble myself to elevate her; and therefore when Hashem questioned him: “Have you eaten of the tree,” he answered: “The woman whom You gave to be with me.”

column11: Eruvin 19a: ‘If the golden altar in the Temple, which was only covered by gold the thickness of a golden dinar, stood for many years and the fire did not burn it, for its gold did not melt, so too the sinners of the Jewish people, who are filled with good deeds like a pomegranate, as it is stated: “Your temples [rakatekh] are like a split pomegranate behind your veil” (Song of Songs 6:7), will not be affected by the fire of Gehenna. And Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said about this: Do not read: Your temples [rakatekh], but rather: Your empty ones [reikateikh], meaning that even the sinners among you are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate; how much more so should the fire of Gehenna have no power over them.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Eruvin 19a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and although he sins in deed whereby he is labeled wicked, nevertheless "even the sinners of Israel are filled with remorse" (Eruvin 19a); and a single thought of remorse in the heart suffices to...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And the final physical execution through the limbs of action counters Envy, which is triggered only when a deed materializes into observable reality visible to another. For this is the root of envy in interpersonal matters, and torts (mili d'nezikin) operate through concrete action driven by evil; and opposite to it in goodness is the practice of benevolence, residing within the Camp of Israel, as our Sages stated (Eruvin 19a and elsewhere): even the transgressors of Israel are as full of mitzvot as a pomegranate.
column15: And this is “He declared the power of His works to His people”—that the Blessed Name imparted to His people the inward vitality and soul of every holy action. For within every mitzvah rests a specific divine intention, yet man is unable by himself to comprehend the full depth of that intention; therefore the Blessed Name granted Israel the physical performance of the mitzvot, so that through the deed itself one assimilates a holiness far exceeding his intellectual understanding.

column11: Kiddushin 49b: ‘If one says to a woman: Be betrothed to me on the condition that I am a righteous man, then even if he was a completely wicked man she is betrothed, as perhaps in the meantime he had thoughts of repentance in his mind and is now righteous. Similarly, if one says to a woman: Be betrothed to me on the condition that I am a wicked man, then even if he was a completely righteous man she is betrothed, as perhaps he had thoughts of idol worship in his mind, a serious sin that would earn him the label of wicked.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Kiddushin 49b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and a single thought of remorse in the heart suffices to render him a consummate tzaddik (Kiddushin 49b); and there is no Jewish sinner who does not regret his deed for a moment once the physical...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And it was already mentioned above from that passage [Kiddushin 49b] that there is no wicked person in any sin who is not reckoned a complete tzaddik through a mere thought of repentance in the heart in a single moment, for there it stated categorically "even a completely wicked person," implying regarding all sins in the world without a single exception; and also [in Niddah 13a] it calls him "wicked for a single hour before the Omnipresent," and it implies that the meaning is because there he did not come intentionally to do wickedness and transgress at all, but only that through holding the organ we suspect he may become heated and arrive at…
column15: For “heavens” alludes to the mind/brain, and within the mind there is no static, fixed order, as novel thoughts arise every single instant; therefore it is not written past-tense “He founded / konanta,” but rather “konen” (He establishes) in the continuous present, meaning that at every successive moment He establishes it anew.

column11: Sanhedrin 44a: ‘§ When God explained to Joshua the reason for the Jewish people’s defeat at the city of Ai, He said: “Israel has sinned” (Joshua 7:11). column11: Sanhedrin 104b: ‘The Gemara adds: Those who interpret the Torah metaphorically would say: All of those enumerated who have no share ultimately enter the World-to-Come, as it is stated: “Gilead is Mine, and Manasseh is Mine, and Ephraim also is the strength of My head; Judah is My scepter; Moab is My washing pot; over Edom I will cast My shoe; Philistia, cry aloud because of Me” (Psalms 60:9–10, and see 108:9–10). “Gilead is Mine and Manasseh is Mine”; this is referring to Ahab, who fell in Ramoth Gilead. “Manasseh”, in its plain meaning, is referring to King Manasseh. “Ephraim also is the strength of My head”; this is referring to Jeroboam, who comes from the tribe of Ephraim. “Judah is My scepter”; this is referring to Ahithophel,’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 104b) to illuminate his exposition here (“so that even regarding those of whom the Mishnah states they have no portion in the World to Come, the expounders of hidden allusions (dorshei reshumot) affirm that they do have a portion...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column11: Taanit 11a: ‘With regard to the third section of the verse: “He is just and righteous,” the Sages said: At the hour of a person’s departure to his eternal home, all his deeds are enumerated before him and are rendered visible to him once again, and the deeds themselves say to him: You did such and such, in such and such a place, on such and such a day, and he says: Yes, that is exactly what happened. column11: Zohar, Chayei Sara 3:17-5:23: ‘It is for that reason that a he-goat is offered up on New-Moon days, namely, because that field has been estranged from the Divine King, so that no blessings from that King could rest upon it; so when the other king is enslaved to the field, we may apply the words, “for in the field he found her, etc.” (Deut. 22, 27). Thus when Eve came into the world she attached herself to the serpent, who injected his impurity into her, so that she brought death into the world and to her husband. Then came Sarah, who, though she went down, came up again, and never attached herself to the serpent, as we read, “And Abram went up out of Egypt, he, and his wife, and all that he had” (Gen. 13, 1). Of Noah, too, it is written, “And he drank of the wine, and was drunken; and he was uncovered within his tent” (Gen. 9, 21).’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 11, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Chayei Sara 3:17-5:23) to illuminate his exposition here (“Wherefore the "Book of the Wicked" (Rosh Hashanah 16b), which is outwardly the most degraded, embodies "he who is small is great" (Zohar I, 122b), being in inner truth the most exalted of all;...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
